subject: SIG: deployment mode differences — fallback routing & dataflow

Subject: SIG — short clarifications requested on hosted/dedicated/private routing & dataflow

Jonas,

Thanks for taking SIG prep with us. Our auditors keep flagging the "deployment mode" questions (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private) and specifically ask for one paragraph descriptions that make clear:

- how requests travel (dataflow) under each mode,
- when and how Redwood performs fallback routing to other model variants/regions, and
- where audit logs / request traces and customer telemetry are stored for evidence.

Can you provide a concise explanation we can hand to our audit team (and any supporting artifacts you can attach)? Ideally a single page summary plus any diagrams or control mappings. We have a SIG window next Friday.

Regards,
Sarah Martinez
Director, Security Controls — Acme Health

From: Jonas Weber <jonas@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: SIG — short clarifications requested on hosted/dedicated/private routing & dataflow

Sarah — thanks for the clear ask. Below is a concise, auditor-friendly summary plus pointers to attached artifacts. I kept it intentionally short for your one-page requirement.

One-page summary (use as-is in SIG responses):

Hosted (Redwood API / multi-tenant):
- Dataflow: Customer request -> Redwood public API gateway (TLS 1.2+/mutual TLS optional) -> routing layer selects an appropriate hosted pool -> inference runtime executes model -> token stream returned through gateway.
- Fallback routing: Policy-based (latency SLOs first, then capacity, then cost). If a pool is at capacity or unhealthy, request is routed to a compatible model variant in another pool/region. All fallback decisions are logged with correlation IDs for audit.
- Evidence storage: Request traces, rate/latency metrics, and audit logs are stored in our central telemetry cluster (encrypted at rest with customer keys for enterprise accounts). Access control is role-based and logged.

Dedicated (reserved capacity for a customer):
- Dataflow: Customer traffic is routed to a customer-dedicated GPU pool (single-tenant compute) managed by Redwood. Control plane still orchestrates but customer data is isolated in the dedicated pool.
- Fallback routing: By default, requests are served within the dedicated pool. Fallback to hosted or other dedicated pools can be configured per contract (explicit opt-in) and uses the same policy engine; any cross-pool fallbacks are subject to contractual SLAs and are recorded in the audit trail.
- Evidence storage: Traces and logs for dedicated pools are partitioned per tenant; for enterprise customers, we can ship logs to a customer-managed S3/GCS or a secured Redshift instance.

Private (VPC / on-prem):
- Dataflow: Control plane (optional) coordinates deployments, but inference occurs within the customer-managed network (VPC or on-prem). Network egress is configurable; many customers disable control-plane egress entirely.
- Fallback routing: There is no automatic cross-tenant fallback by default. Any fallback must be explicitly enabled and happens only to pre-approved model images/variants.
- Evidence storage: Audit logs remain inside the customer environment unless the customer opts to export selected telemetry to Redwood for support. For VPC/private installs we provide schema and local collectors for SOC/SIG evidence.

Additional notes (common to all modes):
- Correlation IDs: Every request gets a trace ID that ties request -> routing decision -> model variant -> runtime events; those IDs appear in traces and can be used to reconstruct flows for audits.
- Encryption & keys: In-flight (TLS) and at-rest encryption are standard; enterprise/private customers can supply KMS keys.
- Control mapping: See attached "sig-hosting-controls-matrix.xlsx" for direct SIG question/answer mapping and control owners.
- Diagrams: Attached PDF shows the condensed dataflow and where logs land per mode.

Attachments: redwood-deploy-dataflow-v2.pdf (one-page diagram), sig-hosting-controls-matrix.xlsx, redwood-soc2-report-2027.pdf (SOC 2 summary).

If you want, Marissa can drop a one-paragraph commercial-friendly line about fallbacks in the contract. Evelyn will add a brief technical appendix about runtime caching and KV handling.

Sarah — quick commercial note to help your procurement/audit team:

- Hosted mode: Standard offering; routing fallback across hosted pools is covered under our standard TOS and operational SLOs. No cross-tenant data sharing.
- Dedicated mode: Fallback to hosted is treated as an escalation path and can be disabled; if enabled, it is explicitly listed in the SLA and will only use sanitized model variants approved by the customer.
- Private/VPC: We treat the customer network as authoritative; any Redwood-initiated fallbacks require prior approval and are visible to the customer.

Timeline: We can provide the one-page summary and the diagram today (attached). If you need signed attestations or exports of traces for specific sample requests, please tell us target date/time ranges and we will prepare a bundle. Adding a short technical appendix for the auditors — feel free to paste this into your SIG response under an "engineering detail" section.

Runtime & routing appendix:
- Batching & KV cache: The inference runtime supports request-level and continuous batching; KV cache entries are tenant-scoped. For hosted mode we maintain per-tenant logical caches; a fallback to another pool will warm a local cache on first access but does not expose a tenant's KV to other tenants.
- Model variants: We classify model images as compatible variants (same architecture/tokenizer). Fallback will only select variants from the compatible set; model fingerprints are recorded in the trace.
- Policy engine: Routing decisions evaluate (1) health, (2) latency SLO, (3) configured cost caps, (4) customer opt-in flags. All decision inputs and outputs are emitted as structured audit events.
- Request trace example: see Drive folder (redwood request-trace sample) — it contains a sample trace (JSON) with correlation_id, routing_decision, model_fingerprint, runtime_events. We redacted customer content; the trace shows how to reconstruct the end-to-end flow.
